U.S. oil output flattens as shale revolution matures

U.S. oil production has remained essentially stable over the last year as the industry has focused on controlling costs and maintaining a disciplined approach to investment despite higher prices driven by war in the Middle East. 

Total crude and condensates production increased by just 136,000 barrels per day (b/d) or 1% in June compared with the same month a year earlier, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration.  

Very modest growth is based on revised and more comprehensive data for 2025 from the U.S. Energy Information Administration published on September 1.  

Production from the Lower 48 states excluding federal waters in the Gulf of Mexico increased by less than 90,000 b/d in June compared with a year earlier, the slowest growth since the pandemic ...

Spared you the generic macro slop about long-term S/D balances. Mentioning 5-10 years structural horizon nowadays just puts ADHD liquidity junkies straight to sleep.

Besides i’ve hammered the table on the core uranium thesis enough times to nauseate everyone on the feed—and all of us have likely already made up our minds.

However there is something i'd like to point out on a slightly shorter time horizon. Western utility contracting activity across both spot/term has been in a total coma for 3 straight years, and 2026 is printing the exact same lethargy. 

Even with SPUT sitting completely sidelined and zero speculative front running, both spot and term prints have quietly been grinding up and to the right.

How long do these fuel buyers think they can play ostrich? Japan is pushing restarts through the queue, China is printing gigawatts of nuclear capacity like monopoly money, and every tech hyperscaler on the planet is fiending for baseload electrons (shoutout to the AI monleys).

Secondary supply? That safety blanket got incinerated back in 2023–2024. What’s the play here—like Waiting for Godot, are they going to sit on their hands indefinitely without filling their backlogs, just waiting for future supply that may or may not arrive?

A bored middle schooler running a 3 minute prompt through ChatGPT knows mining is an operational nightmare and guidance downgrades are practically a hard law of physics in this sector.

Well... plenty of uranium guys are playing a chicken game with utilities... And i believe utilities will eventually have to wave the white flag and get dragged out into the market.

Way more comforting than telling ppl to "HODL until 2040," right? lol

#Gold holds near USD 4,400, having traded as high as USD 4,442 during the Asian session, with the market caught between renewed strength in crude oil, rising bond yields and a softer dollar. Ongoing Gulf tensions are keeping oil prices volatile, and today’s renewed strength is feeding into higher inflation expectations and Treasury yields, weighing on bullion. Algorithmic trading is likely amplifying this relationship, with the negative yield impact only partly offset by dollar weakness, particularly against the Japanese yen.

Beyond these short-term cross-market moves, most developments this week are likely to remain sideshows ahead of the US CPI and PPI releases, which will be critical in shaping expectations for the Fed’s September meeting. Meanwhile, underlying demand remains supported by central-bank buying, with the People’s Bank of China adding the most gold to its reserves since 2023 in August, marking a 22nd consecutive month of purchases.

#Commodities
#Copper on the LME extended gains, hitting a record high for a second straight session at USD 14624.5 per tons, supported by persistent market tightness as miners struggle to keep pace with robust demand heading into the annual peak-demand season. Tightness has been exacerbated by large flows of refined metal to the US ahead of a potential tariff announcement. Copper has gained 17% this year, underpinned by a longer-term mismatch between constrained mine supply and growing demand from data centres, renewable energy infrastructure and power grids.

#Crudeoil holds most of last week’s strong gain, with Brent briefly topping USD 98 a barrel on Monday, a six-week high. Iran said an accord with Oman is imminent and will include a temporary safe shipping route, raising questions about how the US may respond after striking Iranian tankers over the weekend. Tehran also warned that vessels face the risk of attack near Oman, highlighting the continued uncertainty surrounding regional shipping and supply flows.

#Wheat futures rebounded on signs Russia remains committed to continuing its war in Ukraine, heightening concerns about prolonged disruptions to grain shipments from the Black Sea. Prices slumped from a three-year high last week ahead of weekend talks between US envoys and President Vladimir Putin on Ukraine, but the meetings ended without any sign of progress
